newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi leader says negotiator working on summit.
newsitem.headline: Burundi leader says negotiator working on summit.

text.p: Burundi's military ruler Pierre Buyoya said on Saturday that Tanzanian mediator Julius Nyerere agreed to work on a regional East African summit to review developments, and that perhaps Burundi could be represented.
The announcement in Bujumbura followed a meeting in Musoma, western Tanzania, between Buyoya and Nyerere, a former Tanzanian president and internationally backed mediator for Burundi.

"President Nyerere agreed to work on a summit of the heads of state of the region in the coming days in order to review the situation and maybe Burundi will be represented at this summit," Buyoya told a news conference at his residence in the capital.
"The summit will be to review the whole situation in Burundi," Buyoya said, adding that the so-called "Arusha Two" decision (on sanctions) would be considered at the meeting.
Buyoya said a date for the summit would be made public in the near future but there was no set place for it yet.

The news represented a breakthrough for Buyoya, who has been pressing for an end to sanctions, first imposed by regional governments at the second Arusha summit on Burundi held six days after a military coup on July 25.
East African states including Tanzania, Kenya, Rwanda and Uganda imposed crippling economic and transport sanctions on the small but densely populated landlocked country.
They demanded a return to constitutional government, the revival of the National Assembly and talks between all-parties including the army and Hutu rebel groups waging a civil war.

Buyoya said he planned to reconstitute the National Assembly soon, but urged foreigners not to interfere in any talks between his government and the main Hutu rebel group, the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD).
"We are going to talk to armed groups, but we ask our partners not to dictate to us how to do it or when to do it," Buyoya told reporters.
Nyerere this week said the decision by senior members of the former ruling Frodebu party members to support CNDD's armed struggle "clarified" Burundi's political situation.

Frodebu, the Hutu party which beat Buyoya in democratic elections in Burundi in 1993, was banned after the coup and all its senior politicians are in exile or hiding in Western embassies in Bujumbura.

Ousted president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya remains in hiding at the American ambassador's residence in Bujumbura, where he fled just before the coup. Buyoya has said he must stay and participate in a three-year transitional process.
"I want to work with Frodebu in the transitional National Assembly, with those who are willing to co-operate. The others can join the CNDD, it's their choice," he said.

The Forces for the Defence of Democracy (FDD), the armed wing of the CNDD, this week battled the Tutsi-dominated army in the hills surrounding the capital for three days, in what it said was a show of strength.
Around 150,000 people have died in Burundi since 1993, when the country's first democratically-elected Hutu president was killed in an attempted army coup.
